config.title: Home Internet in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: What reaches a Berlin flat, how to prove the line is slower than the contract, and what the proof is worth.

items.q: Can I really reduce my internet bill in Germany if the speed is too low?
items.a: Yes. Section 57 of the Telekommunikationsgesetz has given consumers that right since December 2021. When a measured deviation is significant, continuous or regularly recurring, you may **reduce the agreed charge in proportion to the shortfall** or **terminate the contract without notice**. The reduction runs for as long as the fault lasts, and once the breach is proven it keeps running until the provider proves it is delivering properly.

items.q: What counts as proof that my internet is too slow?
items.a: Only the measurement report from the Bundesnetzagentur's **Breitbandmessung Desktop-App**. A browser speed test, a router screenshot or an app reading carries no weight. The campaign needs **10 measurements a day on three different calendar days**, with at least one clear calendar day between measurement days, no more than **14 calendar days** between the first and last day, at least **three hours** between the fifth and sixth measurement of a day and at least **five minutes** between the others.

items.q: Which speed does the law compare my measurements against?
items.a: All three of the figures on your **Vertragsinformationsblatt**. Any one of these makes a claim: 90 per cent of the **maximum** speed is not reached at least once on at least two of the three days; the **normally available** speed is not reached in 90 per cent of the measurements; or the **minimum** speed is undercut at least once on at least two of the three days. The Bundesnetzagentur fixed those tests in its general ruling of 8 December 2021.

items.q: How common is it to get less than the advertised speed?
items.a: Common enough that it is close to normal. In the Bundesnetzagentur's tenth annual broadband report, published **18 June 2026** and covering October 2024 to September 2025, **45.9 per cent** of measuring fixed-line users reached or beat their full contracted download rate and **85.9 per cent** got at least half of it. The report rests on 184,452 valid fixed-line measurements.

items.q: What can I claim when the technician does not turn up or the line stays down?
items.a: A missed service or installation appointment is worth **€10 or 20 per cent of your monthly charge**, whichever is higher, per appointment. A fault that is not fixed within two calendar days of being reported is worth **€5 or 10 per cent** for the third and fourth day and **€10 or 20 per cent** from the fifth day, for each day of complete outage. A provider switch may leave you offline for at most **one working day**; every further working day is **€10 or 20 per cent**. None of it is paid automatically, so claim it in writing.

items.q: Can my Berlin landlord still charge cable television through the service charges?
items.a: No. The Nebenkostenprivileg ran out with **30 June 2024**, so since 1 July 2024 a monthly broadband or cable basic fee may not be passed to residential tenants through the Betriebskostenabrechnung. A **Glasfaserbereitstellungsentgelt** for a newly fitted fibre installation in the building is still allowed, capped at **€60 a year** and **€540 in total** per dwelling, for at most five years and nine in exceptional cases.

items.q: Is fibre available in Berlin yet?
items.a: Partly. The Berlin Senate's figure of **4 March 2026** is that **53.4 per cent** of households and business premises are passed by fibre, up 12.6 percentage points in a year and ahead of the federal average of 42.9 per cent, with the city aiming for full coverage by **2028**. Counting coaxial cable too, **96.2 per cent** of Berlin is gigabit-capable. Check the exact address on the Bundesnetzagentur's Breitbandatlas before you believe a provider's availability checker.

items.q: What happens to my internet contract when I move flat in Berlin?
items.a: Under section 60 of the Telekommunikationsgesetz the provider must continue the contract at the new address **unchanged**, on the same term and conditions, wherever it offers service there, and the move fee may not be higher than its own charge for a new connection. If it cannot serve the new address, you may terminate with **one month's notice**. Separately, a consumer contract may run for at most 24 months initially, and after the first term ends you can cancel at any time with one month's notice, free of charge.
